title: Responsibilities of operators and end users

opening.headline: If a user causes a problem with the service we created, who will be responsible and to what extent?
body: The moment a service is created with a model API and provided to general users, the story is divided into three parties. These are the provider that created the model, our company that created the service, and the end user who uses the service. If a user creates a result that violates the policy through the service, the responsibilities of all three entities become intertwined.

In this lesson, you will see how policy and behavioral principles documents define and oblige operators and end users, respectively. We then look at how obligations increase in high-risk cases, such as services to minors, and follow with commentary on how to determine liability in cases of user violations and how to design terms of service.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the division of responsibilities between operators and end users
It is possible to distinguish between cases where responsibility lies with the operator and cases where the responsibility lies with the user.

screens.title: If a user causes a problem with the service we created
screens.lead:
Read the situation below and first think about who is responsible for this incident.

Policy base date: 2026-10-23. Distinguish between the version currently in effect and the version scheduled to be implemented. Anthropic has released the 2026-11-12 enforcement version, so you should check again for changes in the enforcement date and high-risk areas and disclosure obligations before actual operation.

visual.alt: A flow chart with three columns: model provider, our company, and end users.

paragraphs: Suppose our company creates a customer service service using a model API and provides it to general users. One day, a user used the service to create phrases to harass others. Is this a violation of the model provider's policy, our company's negligence in management, or the user's personal fault?

It is difficult to determine which of the three is responsible. The provider enforces the policy and monitoring, the service creator manages the policy to ensure that it is followed within the service, and the user must adhere to the terms and policies. The starting point for this lesson is that responsibilities are divided.

To accurately explain the divided responsibilities, we must first distinguish who is the operator and who is the end user. These two terms are used slightly differently in different documents, so the demonstration compares the definitions in each document.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If we write “user responsibility” in the terms and conditions, will our company be free from responsibility? We answer this question in the lesson commentary.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our experience with our Terms of Service.

screens.title: How are user responsibilities written into the terms of service?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts appear. The answer will not be submitted, so please think about our services first.

items.prompt: Are there prohibited actions in our Terms of Service?
items.answer: Once you have written down your prohibited activities, the key is how much your list overlaps with the prohibited categories in your provider's policy. If the prohibited activities in the terms and conditions are narrower than the provider's policy, there is a gap where the user can comply with the terms and conditions but violate the provider's policy.

items.prompt: How do you decide to handle accounts when users break the terms?
items.answer: Many services have no set order of actions. Providers also have stages such as contact, use restrictions, suspension, and closure, so it is easier to explain if the measures for our service are set in the same way.

items.prompt: Are the terms and conditions connected to the model provider's policy?
items.answer: It depends on whether you read the provider's policy and wrote down the terms and conditions, or whether you wrote them down separately. Since the operator is the party that has agreed to the provider's policies, the terms and conditions must be consistent with that agreement.

screens.outro: Now let's see how the documentation defines operator and end user.

screens.title: Who is the operator and who is the end user?
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, a summary of the document's definition appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Claude's Constitution describes an operator as a company or individual building products and services through the API, primarily interacting with the model through a system prompt. A user interacts with the model through human turns in the conversation. The operator and user may be different parties, or one developer may fill both roles. The OpenAI Model Spec also distinguishes a developer from a user; when both are present, developer messages have higher authority. The operator is often not monitoring in real time during a conversation, making advance instructions and operating procedures important.

terms.tip: A company or individual that creates products and services using model APIs. Constitution explains that operators agree with Anthropic's policies and are responsible for the appropriate use of their platform.
These are instructions where the operator informs the model of roles, restrictions, and information in advance. It is distinct from chat messages sent by the user.
It is the person's turn in the conversation who interacts with the model. The model assumes that a person is talking in real time, unless given a cue.
This is a customer who gives instructions from Model Spec to API. Corresponds to the operator of the Constitution and is at a higher level of authority than the user.

This means that the operator often does not directly monitor the conversation. Therefore, operational procedures such as advance directives, monitoring and reporting channels must ensure that responsibilities are met.

screens.outro: Now that we have the definition, let's see what obligations the policy document places on the operator.

screens.title: Operator obligations clause in policy document
screens.lead: The article below is a compilation of provisions from several documents. Select a highlighted phrase to see what it means for you and your users.

data.text: Anthropic's policy applies not only to app users but also to developers and enterprises using the API, as well as It specifies that even end users of the service are subject to application.. The Constitution states that the operator must agree to the policy and explicitly state Responsible for ensuring that models are used appropriately on their platform. OpenAI considers responsible use a shared priority and explicitly states If you break or circumvent the rules, you may lose access.. Google's policy limits its application to all interactions within Google products. The Gemini API documentation explains the consequences of violation as Action is taken in the following order: contact, temporary usage restriction, temporary suspension, and account closure..

marks.span: It specifies that even end users of the service are subject to application.
marks.note: Anthropic policy does not remove end users from responsibility. Since users are also parties to the policy, responsibility is shared rather than being placed on the operator alone.

marks.span: Responsible for ensuring that models are used appropriately on their platform
marks.note: When an operator agrees to a policy, it is a promise to manage the policy to ensure that it is followed within its service. If you leave the terms and conditions alone, it is difficult to say that you have fulfilled this responsibility.

marks.span: If you break or circumvent the rules, you may lose access.
marks.note: This is the text of the OpenAI policy. Loss of access is also a business risk for operators as it can lead to service interruption.

marks.span: Action is taken in the following order: contact, temporary usage restriction, temporary suspension, and account closure.
marks.note: This is the execution phase of Gemini API. When we notify you of a suspension or closure, we will also provide an appeal link. You can use this as a reference when designing the sequence of actions for our services.

screens.outro: The higher the risk, the more obligations there are. Let’s check with services for minors.

screens.title: Operator obligations in services targeting minors
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what obligations each document imposes on services to minors.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: Anthropic's guidance for organizations serving minors cites age verification systems, content moderation and filtering, monitoring and reporting mechanisms, and safe use guidance materials for minors. The idea is that it is reasonable for the operator closest to the user to take these measures. They must also comply with child protection and privacy regulations such as COPPA, disclose this in public documents, and inform users that they are talking to AI.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI Usage policies prohibit the exploitation, grooming, and exposure of age-inappropriate content to those under the age of 18 under the Keep minors safe section. Separate Under-18 guidance cites monitoring with age-appropriate AI notices, content filters and escalation paths as examples. We advise you not to process personal data of persons under the age of 13 without a no-retention setting.

tabs.label: execution
tabs.body: Anthropic says it periodically checks organizations for compliance and may suspend or terminate accounts if noncompliance rates are high and recommendations are not implemented. OpenAI also writes that it can issue warnings if it fails to demonstrate compliance, and may suspend or revoke access in repeated or severe cases. Ultimately, if the operator fails to fulfill his obligations, sanctions will be placed on the operator's account. Since individual minors who use the service cannot be held responsible, the document places the weight of responsibility on the person who created the service.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the obligations and enforcement structure, let’s determine liability through user violations.

screens.title: Commentary: Operator's responsibility when end user violates policy
screens.lead: Let’s solve the previous counseling chatbot case in four steps. An end user created a post using a chatbot to harass a specific person. Select the next arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Step 1: Determine the type of violation
steps.body: Harassment is a prohibited category under all three company policies. Google puts bullying and intimidation on its ban list, while OpenAI puts threats and harassment on its ban list. Therefore, this incident is classified as a policy violation. If the request was in the allowed category, no further steps are required.

steps.title: Step 2: Check the operator’s preemptive obligation
steps.body: See what we did before the incident occurred. Check whether prohibited actions are written in the terms and conditions, whether there is a monitoring system to detect policy violations, and whether there is a route for users to report them. These three are part of the operator's preemptive obligations.

steps.title: Step 3: Follow up
steps.body: If a violation is confirmed, we will restrict the account, keep a record of the incident, and use the provider's reporting channels if necessary. Actions are taken in stages from contact to restriction and suspension, just like the enforcement stage for a provider, but if it is a serious violation, it is written down in the terms and conditions so that a higher level can be applied immediately.

steps.title: Step 4: Determine responsibility
steps.body: If you have fulfilled your preemptive obligations and have also taken reactive actions, this incident will be isolated to an individual user's violation. Conversely, if there is no monitoring or reporting route, there is a risk that the operator's account may be sanctioned due to the operator's negligence in management. The mere fact that it is written in the terms and conditions that it is the user's responsibility does not change this judgment. These four steps can be used as a checklist not only when an incident occurs, but also when designing a service.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the order of responsibility, let's look at how to translate this into terms and conditions and operating procedures.

screens.title: Commentary: How to Link to Terms of Service
screens.lead: Click the toggle to compare how the same incident is handled differently when there are only terms and conditions and when operational procedures are added to the terms and conditions.

states.label: If there are only terms and conditions
states.body: Prohibited actions are written in the terms and conditions, but there is no monitoring or reporting channel. A user's harassing post is not discovered until the victim first reports it to the outside world. Even after discovery, there are no standards for action, so response is delayed, and account processing also varies depending on the person in charge. The mere fact that there are terms and conditions does not eliminate the operator's obligations, so from the provider's perspective, it may appear as a poorly managed service. If the same incident is repeated, the risk of being judged to have a high violation rate also increases.

states.label: Terms and operating procedures
states.body: The Prohibited Conduct provisions in the Terms and Conditions mirror the common prohibited categories in the Provider's policies. In case of violation, actions are taken in the order of warning, restriction, and termination in line with the provider's enforcement stage. AI use notices, age conditions, and reporting routes are included in the terms and conditions and on-screen instructions, and monitoring results are checked regularly. When a report is received, we document who handles it and in what order, from receipt to action. This way, when an incident occurs, you can take action according to established procedures and explain based on the records. The difference between the two cases is not the length of the terms and conditions, but whether there is a procedure to actually make the terms and conditions work. You should also check whether the order of actions written in the terms and conditions and the person in charge matches the division of duties of the actual operating department.

screens.outro: Now that I have finished explaining the case, I will summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Those who create services also have obligations
screens.lead: The contents of this class are organized into three parts: liability structure, risk-based obligations, and terms and conditions design.

paragraphs: Responsibilities are divided rather than concentrated in one place. The operator is responsible for appropriate use of its services while agreeing to the provider's policies. Because end users are also subject to the policy, they are also responsible for individual violations. The provider supports this structure with monitoring and enforcement.

Obligations increase with risk. Services targeting minors may require additional measures such as age verification, content filters, monitoring and reporting mechanisms, AI notifications, and compliance with applicable laws. If the operator fails to fulfill this obligation, the provider may issue a warning or suspend access, and the burden will be on the operator's account.

To be effective, terms and conditions reflect policy but must be combined with operating procedures. Prohibited actions reflect common prohibited categories, actions are ordered in the same order as the provider's enforcement steps, and notification and reporting pathways are on-screen. When an incident occurs, a grounded explanation can be provided by checking the order of violation type, preemptive obligation, follow-up action, and judgment of responsibility.

In practice, we recommend organizing the following items on one page before opening the service. What are the operator obligations of our services, which categories of the provider's policies do the prohibited conduct clauses reflect, what is the order of action in case of violations, whether use by minors is possible, and how we inform users of the use of AI. This theorem provides a basis for explaining responsibility when an incident occurs. If you fill out the same items repeatedly every time you open a new service, the operating standards will be less likely to vary from service to service.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Writing that the user is responsible for the terms and conditions does not eliminate the operator's obligations.

checks.intro: Check for yourself how responsibilities are divided. This confirmation is not logged.
checks.q: What is the appropriate responsibility structure when an end user creates a policy violation in a consultation service made with an API?
options: Only the end user is responsible and the operator is irrelevant.
Both operators and end users are subject to the policy, so responsibility is divided.
Only the model provider is responsible.
If prohibited actions are written in the terms and conditions, there are no operator sanctions under any circumstances.
checks.explain: Anthropic's policy applies to both API customers and end users of its services, and operators are responsible for the appropriate use of their platforms.

wrong.0: Since the operator has also agreed to the policy, he or she has a duty to monitor and take action.
wrong.2: The obligation lies with the operator and user who created the service, not the provider.
wrong.3: Terms and conditions are the starting point and require separate operational obligations such as monitoring and action.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The starting point for division of responsibility is that both entities are covered.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This is a view that pushes responsibility to one side. Think again about who your policy covers.

checks.intro: Think about the checking sequence that determines responsibility when a user violation occurs. Arrange the items in the appropriate order.
checks.q: Arrange them in an appropriate order to determine operator responsibility when an end-user violation occurs.
items: Check if the violation type is a prohibited category
Check preemptive obligations such as terms and conditions, monitoring, and reporting channels.
Take follow-up measures such as account restrictions and record preservation.
Liability is judged based on whether the preemptive obligation is fulfilled.
checks.explain: Liability is determined after reviewing the type of violation, preemptive obligations, and follow-up actions. If the preemptive obligation has been fulfilled, it will be separated into individual user violations.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. This is the process of determining responsibility after fact-checking and inspection.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. Think about what you need to check before determining liability.

checks.intro: Check out how we design our terms and conditions. Just choose the explanation that best suits you.
checks.q: What is the right way to design terms of service?
options: If there are terms and conditions, there is no need for separate operating procedures.
User violations are subject to immediate termination without any steps.
Prohibited actions are newly determined according to our industry, and the provider policy is for reference only.
Prohibited actions reflect common prohibited categories, and actions are ordered in the same order as the provider enforcement steps.
checks.explain: The terms and conditions should reflect the common prohibited categories of the provider's policy and align the order of actions, but have separate operating procedures.

wrong.0: The terms and conditions alone do not eliminate the operator's obligations.
wrong.1: Since provider enforcement progresses to warning, restriction, suspension, and closure, it is appropriate to follow the order.
wrong.2: Common prohibited categories must be reflected as is to ensure that it does not conflict with the provider's policy.

checks.correctFeedback: Good. It is designed to consistently align with the provider's policies and terms and conditions.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This approach may run counter to provider policy or lead to missed operational obligations. Rethink the relationship between terms and policies.

glossary.def: A company or individual that creates a product using an API and provides it to end users.
This is the person who actually uses the operator's services. Included in policy coverage.
Responsibilities are divided between the provider, operator, and end user according to their respective roles.
It is a matter of reflecting the prohibited categories and enforcement methods of the provider's policy in its service terms and operating procedures.

misconceptions.myth: The provider's policy is between the provider and us and has nothing to do with the user.
misconceptions.fact: Anthropic policies extend to end users of the service.

misconceptions.myth: If the terms and conditions state that the user is responsible, the operator is exempted from liability.
misconceptions.fact: The operator's obligations, such as monitoring and notification, remain separate from the Terms and Conditions.

misconceptions.myth: Obligations for minors are in accordance with the law and are unrelated to the provider's guidelines.
misconceptions.fact: Providers also check an organization's compliance and may suspend or terminate accounts if noncompliance rates are high.

closing.lead: We recapitulate the key points of this lesson.
points: Those who create services also have obligations.
End users are also subject to policies.
The greater the risk, the greater the operator's obligations.
It has terms and conditions and operating procedures.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What do we, as operators, have to do when a user violates our policies on our service?
